Random weights; XOR and sum hashing.

Hashing sets with random weights: give every value v a random 64-bit weight r(v). Then the multiset of a segment is summarised by Σ r(ai) (sum hashing) or ⊕ r(ai) (XOR hashing), both available from prefix sums in O(1). XOR cancels pairs, so "every value appears an even number of times" ⇔ prefix XORs are equal at both ends.

Sum hashing checks "is this segment a permutation of 1 … k" (compare with Σ r(1..k)), "do two segments contain the same multiset", and graph conditions like "every vertex has exactly one outgoing edge" (星战

text: Counts subarrays in which every value occurs an even number of times; checked by testing every subarray in Python.
With plain values instead of random weights, 1 ⊕ 2 ⊕ 3 = 0 would wrongly look "even". Random weights make such accidents practically impossible.
Shifts and ORs 64 at a time.

Bitset optimisation: a std::bitset packs 64 booleans per machine word, so shifts, OR, AND and counting run 64 times faster than a bool loop. Subset-sum feasibility: reach |= reach << w for each weight, O(n·S / 64). Transitive closure: if i reaches k then row i |= row k, O(n³ / 64). Gaussian elimination mod 2 XORs whole rows.

The size of a bitset must be a compile-time constant: declare it for the maximum S. Combining bitsets with Mo's algorithm answers "are there two values in the range with difference / sum / product d" (小清新人渣的本愿 P3674).
How many totals from 0 to S can be formed by a subset of the weights; checked with a Python set of reachable sums.
reach.count() counts all set bits at once; (reach >> k)._Find_first() style tricks find the next reachable value. With weights up to 10⁵ and n = 10⁴ this is about 1.5·10⁷ word operations.
Stack DFS; blocks of size B..3B with capitals.

Tree blocking (树分块 , 王室联邦 P2325): cut a tree into blocks of size between B and 3B, each with a "capital" such that every block vertex reaches the capital inside the block (the capital itself may lie outside). DFS with a stack: after each child returns, if more than B vertices were pushed since entering u, pop them as one block with capital u. Push u last; leftovers (fewer than B) join the last block.

With B = √n this gives O(√n) blocks of size O(√n) and short paths between capitals: the base of Mo's algorithm on trees with a block order, and of "precompute answers between capitals" methods for path queries.
The answer is not unique, so the output is checked by a validator in Python: every block has between B and 3B vertices, and block ∪ {capital} is connected in the tree.
The Luogu problems for this chapter, a ladder through them, and experiments to try yourself.
Key points to memorise
1. 根号分治 : x ≤ √n ⇒ precomputed table; x > √n ⇒ ≤ √n direct terms.
2. Degree split: few heavy vertices (deg > √m), many cheap light ones.
3. Set hash: random 64-bit weight per value; XOR for parity, sum for multisets.
4. bitset: reach |= reach << w; closure row |= row; n/64 speed-up.
5. Tree blocking: pop ≥ B stacked vertices after a child; capital = current vertex.
